Authorities

The cases and statutes I cite, each with the official opinion and a short note on what it decides and why it matters to an owner of a closely held business.

New Jersey

  • Namerow v. PediatriCare Associates, LLC 461 N.J. Super. 133, 218 A.3d 839 (Ch. Div. 2018)

    An unambiguous operating agreement valuation provision is enforced as written. Sixteen years of contrary practice did not modify it, and a fiduciary duty claim could not be used to obtain a valuation methodology the member had not bargained for.

  • Balsamides v. Protameen Chemicals, Inc. 160 N.J. 352, 734 A.2d 721 (1999)

    A marketability discount may be applied in an oppression buyout when equity requires it. Where the oppressor is the seller and the oppressed shareholder is the buyer, applying the discount prevents the oppressor from receiving a windfall and recognizes the illiquidity the buyer will bear.

  • Lawson Mardon Wheaton, Inc. v. Smith 160 N.J. 383, 734 A.2d 738 (1999)

    A marketability discount ordinarily should not be applied in determining the fair value of dissenting shareholders' stock absent extraordinary circumstances. A later arm's-length acquisition price may be considered as evidence of value even when it postdates the valuation date by several years.

  • N.J.S.A. 14A:11-1 to -11 — Dissenters' Rights N.J.S.A. 14A:11-1 to -11

    The New Jersey appraisal statute gives qualifying dissenting shareholders a procedure to demand payment of the fair value of their shares following specified corporate actions, with judicial appraisal available when the parties do not agree on value.

  • N.J.S.A. 42:2C-48 — Judicial Dissolution and Alternative Remedies N.J.S.A. 42:2C-48

    A court may dissolve a New Jersey limited liability company on statutory grounds including unlawful or impracticable operations and oppressive conduct directly harmful to a member, or order another remedy—including a sale of a member's interest—when that relief is fair and equitable.

  • N.J.S.A. 14A:12-7 — Involuntary Dissolution and Alternative Remedies N.J.S.A. 14A:12-7

    In qualifying closely held corporations, the court may grant dissolution or alternative equitable relief for deadlock, illegality, fraud, abuse, waste, or oppression, including an order that the corporation or other shareholders purchase a shareholder's stock at fair value.

New York

  • Ferolito v. AriZona Beverages USA LLC 2014 N.Y. Slip Op. 32830(U) (Sup. Ct. Nassau Cnty. Oct. 14, 2014)

    In valuing an interest in the AriZona beverage enterprise, the trial court relied principally on a DCF analysis, declined to treat unconsummated expressions of interest as reliable transaction value, and applied a 25% marketability discount based on multiple company-specific illiquidity risks.

  • Friedman v. Beway Realty Corp. 87 N.Y.2d 161, 661 N.E.2d 972, 638 N.Y.S.2d 399 (1995)

    Fair value measures a dissenting shareholder's proportionate interest in the value of the enterprise. A discount based on the shares' minority status may not be applied.

  • New York Business Corporation Law § 1118 N.Y. Bus. Corp. Law § 1118

    After a qualifying dissolution petition, the corporation or other shareholders may make an irrevocable election to purchase the petitioner's shares at fair value, ordinarily measured as of the day before the petition was filed and without value created by the filing itself.

Delaware

  • Verition Partners Master Fund Ltd. v. Aruba Networks, Inc. 210 A.3d 128 (Del. 2019)

    On the record presented, the Court of Chancery abused its discretion by using Aruba's unaffected thirty-day trading price. Fair value was the arm's-length deal price minus the portion attributable to merger synergies.

  • M.P.M. Enterprises, Inc. v. Gilbert 731 A.2d 790 (Del. 1999)

    Merger price and prior offers may be relevant in appraisal, but the Court of Chancery may give them no weight when the proponent fails to connect them to the company's going-concern value rather than buyer-specific or merger-created synergies.

  • Cavalier Oil Corp. v. Harnett 564 A.2d 1137 (Del. 1989)

    Appraisal values the corporation as an operating entity and awards the dissenter a proportionate interest in that going concern; a shareholder-level minority or marketability discount is improper.

  • 8 Del. C. § 262 — Appraisal Rights 8 Del. C. § 262

    A qualifying stockholder may obtain judicial appraisal of fair value; the Court of Chancery must consider all relevant factors while excluding value arising from the accomplishment or expectation of the merger or consolidation.

Federal

  • Revenue Ruling 59-60 Rev. Rul. 59-60, 1959-1 C.B. 237

    When market quotations are unavailable, the fair market value of closely held stock is determined from all available financial data and all relevant factors under the hypothetical willing-buyer and willing-seller standard; no single formula controls.
